front: Ability: be able to vs can
back: Avoid 'be able to' for things happening as we speak; use 'can' instead [7].
Prefer 'can' (e.g., 'Films can now easily be streamed') [7].
Prefer 'can' over 'are you able to' (e.g., 'Can you cook?') [7].
Use 'was able to' (not 'could') for specific successful attempts [7].
'Could not' is usually more natural than 'was not able to' [7].
Use 'could' (e.g., feel, hear, see, smell, taste, believe, remember) [7].
Use 'can' for very real possibility; 'could' suggests less likely or doubt [7].

front: She swam strongly and ... cross the river.
All we ... see were his feet.

back: could nearly (to suggest something almost happened) [7].
